title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 11–13 (Night 225, continuing nights-224), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 225 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Opening the bundles, the king finds in each son's pocket a letter and locks of hair from his own wives, Budūr and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, and realises he has had his sons killed for nothing. He strikes his face and laments, builds two tombs in a “House of Sorrows”, recites a poem over each, and shuts himself away there, giving up his wives and friends. Meanwhile al-Amjad and al-Asʿad wander the wilderness for a month to a mountain of black flint; they climb its upper road for five exhausting days without reaching the end, then turn back and take the road through its middle, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-fifth night,
sentences.n: As at every night's opening: the unit, al-khāmisatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, and both stand in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا فَتَحَ الْبُقْجَتَيْنِ وَصَارَ يُقَلِّبُ ثِيَابَ أَوْلَادِهِ وَيَبْكِي فَلَمَّا فَتَحَ ثِيَابَ وَلَدِهِ الْأَسْعَدِ وَجَدَ فِي جَيْبِهِ وَرَقَةً مَكْتُوبَةً بِخَطِّ زَوْجَتِهِ بُدُورَ وَفِيهَا جَدَائِلُ شَعْرِهَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Qamara al-Zamāni lammā fataḥa al-buqjatayni wa-ṣāra yuqallibu thiyāba awlādihi wa-yabkī fa-lammā fataḥa thiyāba waladihi al-Asʿadi wajada fī jaybihi waraqatan maktūbatan bi-khaṭṭi zawjatihi Budūra wa-fīhā jadāʾilu shaʿrihā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that King Qamar al-Zamān, when he-opened the-two-bundles and-began he-turns-over (the) clothes (of) his-children and-he-weeps — and-when he-opened (the) clothes (of) his-son al-Asʿad, he-found in his-pocket a-paper written in-(the)-hand (of) his-wife Budūr, and-in-it (the) braids (of) her-hair.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when King Qamar al-Zamān had opened the two bundles and was turning his sons' clothes over and weeping, he opened the clothes of his son al-Asʿad, and found in the pocket a letter written in the hand of his wife Budūr, with locks of her hair inside it.
sentences.n: The print has اولادة and ولدة, misprints for اولاده and ولده, corrected here. As in the night before, the print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set and read as the two words al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”. The first lammā, “when”, never gets its answer: the storyteller starts again with fa-lammā, “and when”, and only that second clause is completed, by wajada, “he found”. The broken sentence is the spoken style and is kept. Qamara al-Zamāni stands in apposition to al-malika, the accusative noun of anna. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to”, as at the end of the night before. jayb, “pocket”, properly the opening at the breast of a garment, where things were carried. waraqa, “leaf, sheet of paper”, here a letter; maktūbatan agrees with it. bi-khaṭṭi, “in the handwriting of”: bi- marks the hand it was written in. Budūra is a diptote, so its genitive ends in -a. jadāʾil, plural of jadīla, “plait, braid”; wa-fīhā jadāʾilu shaʿrihā, “with the braids of her hair in it”, is a circumstantial clause. The letter in al-Asʿad's clothes is from Budūr, al-Amjad's mother: each stepmother had written to the other's son. The shadda of يقلّب and the ئ of جدائل are printed.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَ الْوَرَقَةَ وَقَرَأَهَا وَفَهِمَ مَعْنَاهَا فَعَلِمَ أَنَّ وَلَدَهُ الْأَسْعَدَ مَظْلُومٌ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥa al-waraqata wa-qaraʾahā wa-fahima maʿnāhā fa-ʿalima anna waladahu al-Asʿada maẓlūmun
sentences.l: So-he-opened the-paper and-read-it and-understood its-meaning, and-so-he-knew that his-son al-Asʿad (was) wronged.
sentences.i: He unfolded the letter and read it and understood what it meant, and he knew that his son al-Asʿad had been wronged.
sentences.n: The print has ولدة, a misprint for ولده, corrected here. fa- runs the steps on one out of another: he opened, read, understood, and so knew. maʿnā, “meaning, sense”, with -hā, the letter's. maẓlūm, passive participle of ẓalama, “wronged, treated unjustly”, stands as the predicate of anna in the nominative, while waladahu al-Asʿada, its noun, is accusative. The أ of قرأها is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَتَّشَ رِزْمَةَ الْأَمْجَدِ فَوَجَدَ فِي جَيْبِهِ وَرَقَةً مَكْتُوبَةً بِخَطِّ زَوْجَتِهِ حَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ وَفِيهَا جَدَائِلُ شَعْرِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma fattasha rizmata al-Amjadi fa-wajada fī jaybihi waraqatan maktūbatan bi-khaṭṭi zawjatihi Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi wa-fīhā jadāʾilu shaʿrihā
sentences.l: Then he-searched (the) bundle (of) al-Amjad, and-found in his-pocket a-paper written in-(the)-hand (of) his-wife Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, and-in-it (the) braids (of) her-hair.
sentences.i: Then he searched al-Amjad's bundle, and found in the pocket a letter written in the hand of his wife Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, with locks of her hair inside it.
sentences.n: fattasha, Form II of f-t-sh, “to search through”, here with a direct object; its shadda, فتّش, is printed. rizma, “bundle, package”, another word for the buqja of the night before. Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi, “Life of Souls”, stands in apposition to zawjatihi and shares its genitive. The second discovery is told in the very words of the first, as storytellers do. The ئ of جدائل is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَ الْوَرَقَةَ وَقَرَأَهَا فَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُ مَظْلُومٌ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥa al-waraqata wa-qaraʾahā fa-ʿalima annahu maẓlūmun
sentences.l: So-he-opened the-paper and-read-it, and-so-he-knew that-he (was) wronged.
sentences.i: He unfolded the letter and read it, and knew that this son too had been wronged.
sentences.n: annahu, “that he”: the suffix -hu is al-Amjad. The أ of قرأها is printed.

sentences.t: فَدَقَّ يَدًا عَلَى يَدٍ وَقَالَ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللّٰهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ قَدْ قَتَلْتُ أَوْلَادِي ظُلْمًا
sentences.tr: fa-daqqa yadan ʿalā yadin wa-qāla lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi qad qataltu awlādī ẓulman
sentences.l: So-he-struck a-hand upon a-hand and-said: No power and-no strength except in-God, the-High, the-Mighty! I-have killed my-children (in) wrong.
sentences.i: He struck one hand upon the other and said: There is no power and no strength save in God, the High, the Mighty! I have put my sons to death unjustly.
sentences.n: daqqa yadan ʿalā yadin, “he struck hand on hand”, the gesture of despair and regret; its shadda, فدقّ, is printed. lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi, “there is no power and no strength but in God”, the formula spoken at a calamity: lā takes its noun in the accusative without tanwīn, and bi- marks God as the one in whom all power lies. The print sets lā ḥawla and wa-lā quwwata each as one word, لاحول ولاقوة; they are kept as set. qad with the perfect, “I have indeed killed”; the ḍamma of قتلتُ is printed. ẓulman, “wrongfully”, an accusative of manner, as in the night before.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَارَ يَلْطِمُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ وَيَقُولُ وَا وَلَدَاهْ وَاطُولَ حُزْنَاهْ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣāra yalṭimu ʿalā wajhihi wa-yaqūlu wā waladāh wā ṭūla ḥuznāh
sentences.l: Then he-began he-slaps on his-face and-he-says: O-alas (my) son! O-alas (the) length (of) my-grief!
sentences.i: Then he fell to beating his face, crying: Alas, my son! Alas, how long my grief!
sentences.n: The print has حزناة, a misprint for حزناه, corrected here. laṭama, “to slap, beat (the face)”, the mourner's gesture; ʿalā marks where the blows fall. wā … -āh is the cry of lament (nudba): wā calls on the one mourned, and the ending -āh, held with a pausal hāʾ, draws out the wail; so wā waladāh, “alas, my son!”, and wā ṭūla ḥuznāh, “alas for the length of my grief!”. The print runs wā and ṭūla together, واطول; kept as set. The father cries “my son” in the singular though he has lost two.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ بِبِنَاءِ قَبْرَيْنِ فِي بَيْتٍ وَاحِدٍ وَسَمَّاهُ بَيْتَ الْأَحْزَانِ وَقَدْ كَتَبَ عَلَيْهِمَا اسْمَيْ وَلَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara bi-bināʾi qabrayni fī baytin wāḥidin wa-sammāhu bayta al-aḥzāni wa-qad kataba ʿalayhimā ismay waladayhi
sentences.l: And-he-commanded with-(the)-building (of) two-tombs in one house, and-named-it (the) House (of) the-Sorrows; and-he-had written upon-them-two (the) two-names (of) his-two-sons.
sentences.i: He gave orders for two tombs to be built in a single house, and named it the House of Sorrows, and he had the names of his two sons written upon them.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes the thing commanded with bi-, here bi-bināʾi, “the building of”; the ء of ببناء is printed. sammā, Form II of s-m-w, “to name”, takes two objects, the thing named, -hu, and the name, bayta al-aḥzāni. Bayt al-Aḥzān, “the House of Sorrows”, is the name tradition gives to the place where Jacob mourned Joseph. wa-qad kataba, “and he had written”: qad with the perfect in a circumstantial clause; kataba stands for having it done. kataba ʿalā, “to write on”: ʿalā marks the surface. ismay waladayhi, “the two names of his two sons”: two duals in construct, both in the oblique case with the nūn dropped; the fatḥa of اسمَي is printed. The shadda of وسمّاه is printed.

sentences.t: وَتَرَامَي عَلَى قَبْرِ الْأَمْجَدِ وَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-tarāmā ʿalā qabri al-Amjadi wa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And-he-threw-himself upon (the) tomb (of) al-Amjad, and-wept, and-moaned, and-complained, and-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then he threw himself upon al-Amjad's tomb, and wept and moaned and lamented, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: tarāmā, Form VI of r-m-y, “to throw oneself down”; ʿalā marks where. The print writes it with a final ي, وترامي, where the same verb after the poem has ى; it is pointed وَتَرَامَي and read tarāmā. anna, yaʾinnu, “to moan”; its shadda, وانّ, is printed. ishtakā, Form VIII of sh-k-w, “to complain”, here of his lot. bakā, anna, ishtakā and then anshada, “he recited (verse)”, are the storyteller's usual run before a poem; hādhihi al-abyāta, “these verses”, is its object.

sentences.t:
يَاقَمَرًا قَدْ غَابَ تَحْتَ الثَّرَى * بَكَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْاَنْجُمُ الزَّاهِرَةْ
وَيَا قَضِيبًا لَمْ يَمُسَّ بَعْدَهُ * مَعَاطِفَ لِلْأَعْيُنِ النَّاظِرَةْ
مَنَعْتُ عَيْنِي عَنْكَ مِنْ غَيْرَتِي * عَلَيْكَ حَتَّى صِرْتُ لِلْآخِرَةْ
وَاَغْرَقْتُ بِالسُّهْدِ فِي دَمْعِهَا * وَاِنَّنِي مِنْ ذَاكَ بِالسَّاهِرَةْ
sentences.tr:
yā qamaran qad ghāba taḥta al-tharā * bakat ʿalayhi al-anjumu al-zāhirah
wa-yā qaḍīban lam yamussa baʿdahu * maʿāṭifa li-al-aʿyuni al-nāẓirah
manaʿtu ʿaynī ʿanka min ghayratī * ʿalayka ḥattā ṣirtu li-al-ākhirah
wa-aghraqtu bi-al-suhdi fī damʿihā * wa-innanī min dhāka bi-al-sāhirah
sentences.l:
O moon (that) has set beneath the-soil, * wept over-him the-stars, the-shining!
And-O bough (that) not touched after-him * bends for-the-eyes, the-looking!
I-kept-back my-eye from-you out-of my-jealousy * over-you, until I-became for-the-hereafter;
and-I-drowned (it) with-the-sleeplessness in its-tears, * and-indeed-I from that (am) at-the-Sāhira.
sentences.i:
O moon that has set beneath the earth, * the shining stars have wept for him!
O bough, since whom no graceful form * has swayed before the watching eyes!
I kept my eyes from you, so jealous was I * for you, until I was bound for the world to come;
I drowned my eye in its tears through sleepless nights, * and so I stand already on the plain of waking.
sentences.n: Four lines in the metre sarīʿ, rhyming in -irah, the closing tāʾ marbūṭa held in pause, as the printed sukūn on الزَّاهِرَةْ and its fellows shows. The print runs yā and qamaran together, يَاقَمَرًا; kept as set. The dead son is a moon set beneath al-tharā, “the moist earth, the soil”, and a qaḍīb, “a slender bough”, the stock image of a graceful youth; ʿalayhi, “over him”, moves from address to the third person, as Arabic verse freely does. Line 2 is doubtful as printed: yamussa, “touch”, gives the half-line one syllable too many and makes hard sense; metre and image point to yamis, “sway”, from māsa, yamīsu, “to sway proudly”: “a bough after whom no flanks have swayed for the watching eyes”. The print is kept, and the idiomatic line follows that likelier sense. maʿāṭif, plural of miʿṭaf, “the bends of the body, the flanks”, is a diptote and printed without tanwīn; the metre wants a tanwīn, and on the yamis reading, where the flanks are what sway, the word would be nominative, maʿāṭifun. min ghayratī ʿalayka, “out of my jealousy over you”: ghayra is protective, possessive jealousy, and min gives the cause; the father, it seems, kept his eyes off the boy for fear of harming him with his gaze. ṣirtu li-al-ākhirah, “I became for the next world”: li- marks where he is now bound. In line 4 aghraqtu, “I drowned”, has its object, the eye, understood from damʿihā, “its tears”; bi-al-suhdi, “through sleeplessness”, is bi- of cause. bi-al-sāhirah closes with a play: al-sāhira is “the wakeful (eye)”, from sahira, “to stay awake”, and also al-Sāhira, the bare plain where the dead are gathered at the Resurrection (Qurʾān 79:14); bi- marks the place where he is. The first half of line 4 does not scan cleanly as printed. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare, as in الْاَنْجُمُ, وَاَغْرَقْتُ and وَاِنَّنِي, but prints the أ of لِلْأَعْيُنِ and the آ of لِلْآخِرَةْ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَرَامَى عَلَى قَبْرِ الْأَسْعَدِ وَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَي وَأَفَاضَ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma tarāmā ʿalā qabri al-Asʿadi wa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-afāḍa al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he-threw-himself upon (the) tomb (of) al-Asʿad, and-wept and-moaned and-complained and-poured-out the-tears, and-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then he threw himself upon al-Asʿad's tomb, and wept and moaned and lamented, and let his tears flow, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: The same run of verbs as at the first tomb, with one more: afāḍa al-ʿabarāti, “he poured out the tears”, afāḍa being Form IV of f-y-ḍ, “to make overflow”; ʿabarāt is the plural of ʿabra, “tear”. This time tarāmā has its proper ى, and ishtakā is printed with a final ي, واشتكي; it is pointed وَاشْتَكَي and read ishtakā. The shadda of وانّ is printed.

sentences.t:
قَدْ كُنْتُ اَهْوَى اَنْ اُشَاطِرَكَ الرَّدَى * لٰكِنْ اَرَادَ اللّٰهُ غَيْرَ مُرَادِي
سَوَّدْتُ مَا بَيْنَ الْفَضَاءِ وَنَاظِرِي * وَمَحَوْتُ مِنْ عَيْنِي كُلَّ سَوَادِ
لَا يَنْفَدُ الدَّمْعُ الَّذِي اَبْكِي بِهِ * اِنَّ الْفُؤَادَ لَهُ مِنَ الْاِمْدَادِ
اِعْزِزْ عَلَيَّ بِاَنْ اَرَاكَ بِمَوْضِعٍ * مُتَسَاوِيهِ الْاَوْغَادِ وَالْاَمْجَادِ
sentences.tr:
qad kuntu ahwā an ushāṭiraka al-radā * lākin arāda Allāhu ghayra murādī
sawwadtu mā bayna al-faḍāʾi wa-nāẓirī * wa-maḥawtu min ʿaynī kulla sawādi
lā yanfadu al-damʿu alladhī abkī bihi * inna al-fuʾāda lahu mina al-imdādi
iʿziz ʿalayya bi-an arāka bi-mawḍiʿin * mutasāwīhi al-awghādi wa-al-amjādi
sentences.l:
I-had been wishing that I-share-halves-with-you the-death, * but willed God other-than my-willed-thing.
I-blackened what (is) between the-open-air and-my-eye, * and-I-wiped-out from my-eye every blackness.
Not runs-out the-tear which I-weep with-it: * indeed the-heart (has) for-it (some) of the-supply.
How-grievous upon-me that I-see-you in-a-place * equal-in-it the-base-ones and-the-glorious-ones!
sentences.i:
I had longed to share your death with you, * but God willed other than I willed.
I have darkened all between the sky and my eye, * and wiped from my eye all its black.
The tears I weep will never run dry: * the heart keeps them supplied.
How hard it is for me to see you in a place * where the base and the noble lie as equals!
sentences.n: Four lines in the metre kāmil, rhyming in -ādi. ahwā, “I love, desire”, here with an and the subjunctive; shāṭara, Form III, “to go halves with”, so an ushāṭiraka al-radā, “to share death with you half and half”. ghayra murādī, “other than what I willed”: murād, “the thing willed”, plays on arāda, “he willed”. Line 2 plays on black: sawwada, “to blacken”, says the world has gone dark between the open air, al-faḍāʾ, and his eye, and sawād is also the black of the eye, wept away, as Jacob's eyes went white with grief; the second half of the line does not scan cleanly as printed. nafida, yanfadu, “to run out”. abkī bihi, “I weep with it”: bi- marks the tears as the means. imdād, “supply, reinforcement”: the heart keeps feeding the tears; li- in lahu marks the tears as what is supplied. iʿziz ʿalayya bi-an, “how grievous to me that”, is the verb of wonder, the pattern afʿil bi-, from ʿazza ʿalā, “to be hard on”; bi- marks what is wondered at. The print sets a kasra under its alif, اِعْزِزْ, where the pattern has a fatḥa, aʿziz; the printed mark is kept, and the transliteration follows it. mutasāwīhi, as printed, does not scan, since its long -wī- stands where the metre wants a short syllable, and it has no clear grammar; mutasāwiyan, “equal”, would scan, and the sense must be “in which are equal”, mutasāwin fīhi; it is translated in that sense. al-awghād, “the base, the rabble”, and al-amjād, “the glorious”: the poem's last word plays on al-Amjad's name, though the lines are spoken at al-Asʿad's tomb. The print writes the hamza-bearing alifs bare (اَهْوَى, اُشَاطِرَكَ, اَرَادَ, اِنَّ, اِعْزِزْ, الْاِمْدَادِ, الْاَمْجَادِ and others), but prints the ء of الْفَضَاءِ and the ؤ of الْفُؤَادَ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ زَادَ الْمَلِكُ فِى الْبُكَاءِ وَالْأَنِينِ
sentences.tr: thumma zāda al-maliku fī al-bukāʾi wa-al-anīni
sentences.l: Then increased the-king in the-weeping and-the-moaning.
sentences.i: Then the king wept and moaned all the more.
sentences.n: zāda fī, “to increase in, go further in”: fī marks what grows. bukāʾ, “weeping”, and anīn, “moaning”, are the verbal nouns of bakā and anna. The print spells fī with ى, فى; the ء of البكاء is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ بُكَائِهِ وَشِعْرِهِ هَجَرَ الْأَحْبَابَ وَالْخِلَّانَ وَانْقَطَعَ فِي الْبَيْتِ الَّذِي سَمَّاهُ بَيْتَ الْأَحْزَانِ وَصَارَ يَبْكِي فِيهِ عَلَى أَوْلَادِهِ وَقَدْ هَجَرَ نِسَاءَهُ وَأَصْحَابَهُ وَأَصْدِقَاءَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā faragha min bukāʾihi wa-shiʿrihi hajara al-aḥbāba wa-al-khillāna wa-inqaṭaʿa fī al-bayti alladhī sammāhu bayta al-aḥzāni wa-ṣāra yabkī fīhi ʿalā awlādihi wa-qad hajara nisāʾahu wa-aṣḥābahu wa-aṣdiqāʾahu
sentences.l: And-when he-finished from his-weeping and-his-verse, he-forsook the-loved-ones and-the-bosom-friends, and-cut-himself-off in the-house which he-named-it (the) House (of) the-Sorrows, and-began he-weeps in-it over his-children; and-he-had forsaken his-women and-his-companions and-his-friends.
sentences.i: When he had done with his weeping and his verses, he forsook those he loved and his close friends, and shut himself away in the house he had named the House of Sorrows, and there he wept for his sons, having forsaken his wives, his companions and his friends.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to finish with”: min marks what is done with. hajara, “to forsake, keep away from”. aḥbāb, plural of ḥabīb, “loved one”; khillān, plural of khalīl, “bosom friend”, its shadda, الخلّان, printed. inqaṭaʿa fī, Form VII of q-ṭ-ʿ, “to be cut off”, here “to shut oneself away in”: fī marks the place. alladhī sammāhu, “which he named it”: Arabic takes up the relative with a pronoun, -hu, inside its clause; the shadda of سمّاه is printed. bakā ʿalā, “to weep over”: ʿalā marks the ones mourned. wa-qad hajara, “having forsaken”, a circumstantial clause with qad. nisāʾ, “women”, here his wives, Budūr and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs among them. The ئ of بكائه and the ء of نساءه and اصدقاءه are printed.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihi
sentences.l: This (is) what was of his-affair.
sentences.i: So much for him.
sentences.n: The print has امرة, a misprint for امره, corrected here. hādhā mā kāna min amrihi … wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what there was of his affair; and as for what there was of the affair of …”, is the storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the tale and taking up another: min marks the affair as the whole the account is drawn from.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ فَإِنَّهُمَا لَمْ يَزَالَا سَائِرَيْنِ فِي الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَهُمَا يَأْكُلَانِ مِنْ نَبَاتِ الْأَرْضِ وَيَشْرَبَانِ مِنْ مُتَحَصِّلَاتِ الْأَمْطَارِ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ حَتَّى انْتَهَى بِهِمُ الْمَسِيرُ إِلَى جَبَلٍ مِنَ الصَّوَّانِ الْأَسْوَدِ لَا يُعْلَمُ أَيْنَ مُنْتَهَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi fa-innahumā lam yazālā sāʾirayni fī al-barriyyati wa-humā yaʾkulāni min nabāti al-arḍi wa-yashrabāni min mutaḥaṣṣilāti al-amṭāri muddata shahrin kāmilin ḥattā intahā bihimu al-masīru ilā jabalin mina al-ṣawwāni al-aswadi lā yuʿlamu ayna muntahāhu
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad, then-indeed-they-two not ceased travelling in the-wilderness, and-they-two eat from (the) plants (of) the-earth and-drink from (the) gathered-things (of) the-rains, (the) span (of) a-month complete, until ended with-them the-journey at a-mountain of the-flint, the-black, not is-known where (is) its-end.
sentences.i: As for al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, they went on through the wilderness, eating the plants of the earth and drinking what the rains had left standing, for a whole month, until their journey brought them to a mountain of black flint, and no one knew where it ended.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-innahumā, “and as for …, they”: ammā is answered by fa-. lam yazālā sāʾirayni, “they did not cease travelling”: lam yazal with a participle, here in the dual accusative; the ئ of سائرين is printed, and the shadda of البرّية. wa-humā yaʾkulāni, “while they were eating”, a circumstantial clause opened by wa- and a pronoun; the أ of يأكلان is printed. akala min and shariba min: min marks what they lived on, “some of”. mutaḥaṣṣilāt al-amṭār, “what the rains had gathered”, a Form V participle of ḥ-ṣ-l, “to be collected”, used as a noun in the later language: rainwater lying in hollows. muddata shahrin, “for the space of a month”, an adverbial accusative. intahā bihimu al-masīru ilā, “the journey ended with them at”: bi- marks those the journey carries, and ilā where it stops. The pronoun is the plural, bihim, for the two brothers, where Classical Arabic wants the dual bihimā; the spoken language lets the plural stand for two. It takes a ḍamma, bihimu, before the article. ṣawwān, “flint, hard stone”; its shadda, الصوّان, is printed. min al-ṣawwāni, “of flint”: min names the stuff it is made of. lā yuʿlamu, “it is not known”, a passive. muntahā, “end, limit”, a place-noun of Form VIII.

sentences.t: وَالطَّرِيقُ افْتَرَقَتْ عِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ الْجَبَلِ طَرِيقَيْنِ طَرِيقٌ تَشُقُّهُ مِنْ وَسَطِهِ وَطَرِيقٌ صَاعِدَةٌ إِلَى أَعْلَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ṭarīqu iftaraqat ʿinda dhālika al-jabali ṭarīqayni ṭarīqun tashuqquhu min wasaṭihi wa-ṭarīqun ṣāʿidatun ilā aʿlāhu
sentences.l: And-the-road divided at that the-mountain (into) two-roads: a-road cleaves-it from its-middle, and-a-road climbing to its-top.
sentences.i: At that mountain the road divided in two: one road cut through the middle of it, and one climbed to its top.
sentences.n: ṭarīq, “road, way”, is feminine here, as it may be: iftaraqat, tashuqquhu and ṣāʿidatun all agree with it. The noun is set first, wa-al-ṭarīqu iftaraqat, “and the road, it divided”, the order of the spoken language. iftaraqa, Form VIII of f-r-q, “to part, divide”; ṭarīqayni, “(into) two roads”, an accusative saying what it divided into. Then each road is named afresh in the nominative, ṭarīqun … wa-ṭarīqun. shaqqa, “to split, cut through”; its shadda, تشقّه, is printed. min wasaṭihi, “through its middle”: min marks where the road enters. aʿlā, “top”, the elative used as a noun.

sentences.t: فَسَلَكَا الطَّرِيقَ الَّتِي فِي أَعْلَا الْجَبَلِ وَاسْتَمَرَّا سَائِرَيْنِ فِيهَا خَمْسَةَ أَيَّامٍ فَلَمْ يَرَيَا لَهُ مُنْتَهًى
sentences.tr: fa-salakā al-ṭarīqa allatī fī aʿlā al-jabali wa-istamarrā sāʾirayni fīhā khamsata ayyāmin fa-lam yarayā lahu muntahan
sentences.l: So-they-two-took the-road which (is) at (the) top (of) the-mountain, and-continued travelling on-it five days, and-not they-two-saw for-it an-end.
sentences.i: They took the road that led to the top of the mountain, and kept on along it for five days, but they could see no end to it.
sentences.n: salaka, “to go along, take (a road)”, takes the road as a direct object; allatī, the feminine relative, agrees with al-ṭarīq. The print spells aʿlā with a final alif, اعلا, where the usual spelling has ى; it is kept as printed. istamarra, Form X of m-r-r, “to keep on”, with the participle sāʾirayni, “going”; its shadda, استمرّا, is printed, as is the ئ of سائرين. khamsata ayyāmin, “five days”: a numeral from three to ten takes the feminine form with a masculine noun, and the counted noun follows in the genitive plural. lam yarayā, “they did not see”, the jussive dual of raʾā. lahu, “for it”, the mountain: li- marks what the end belongs to. muntahan, the indefinite accusative of muntahā, is written with ى and read with tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ حَصَلَ لَهُمَا الْإِعْيَاءُ مِنَ التَّعَبِ وَلَيْسَا مُعْتَادَيْنِ عَلَى الْمَشْيِ فِي جَبَلٍ وَلَا فِي غَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ḥaṣala lahumā al-iʿyāʾu mina al-taʿabi wa-laysā muʿtādayni ʿalā al-mashyi fī jabalin wa-lā fī ghayrihi
sentences.l: And-had come-about for-them-two the-exhaustion from the-toil, and-they-two-were-not accustomed to the-walking on a-mountain nor on other-than-it.
sentences.i: Weariness had come over them from the toil, for they were not used to walking, on mountains or anywhere else.
sentences.n: ḥaṣala li-, “to befall, come upon”: li- marks the ones it comes to; the later language uses it of any state that overtakes a person. iʿyāʾ, “exhaustion”, verbal noun of Form IV aʿyā; its ء is printed. min al-taʿabi, “from the toil”: min of cause. laysā, the dual of laysa, takes its predicate in the accusative, muʿtādayni. muʿtād, Form VIII participle of ʿ-w-d, “accustomed”: Classical Arabic says iʿtāda al-shayʾa, with a direct object, and the later language iʿtāda ʿalā, as here, where ʿalā marks the habit. wa-lā fī ghayrihi, “nor in any other”: lā carries the negation of laysā on to the second phrase.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا يَئِسَا مِنَ الْوُصُولِ إِلَى مُنْتَهَاهُ رَجَعَا وَسَلَكَا الطَّرِيقَ الَّتِي فِي وَسَطِ الْجَبَلِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā yaʾisā mina al-wuṣūli ilā muntahāhu rajaʿā wa-salakā al-ṭarīqa allatī fī wasaṭi al-jabali
sentences.l: And-when they-two-despaired of the-arriving at its-end, they-two-turned-back and-took the-road which (is) in (the) middle (of) the-mountain.
sentences.i: When they gave up hope of reaching its end, they turned back and took the road that ran through the middle of the mountain.
sentences.n: yaʾisa min, “to despair of”: min marks what is given up; the ئ of يئسا is printed. wuṣūl ilā, “arriving at”, the verbal noun of waṣala, keeps the verb's ilā. rajaʿā, “they two went back”, dual perfect.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
